titleText.es: Leí en un artículo que la ruptura de la simetría electrodébil es la razón por la que tenemos ALMAS. ¡Un tipo con licenciatura lo ha dicho!
titleText.en: I read in this one article that the breaking of electroweak symmetry is the reason we have SOULS. This guy with a degree said so!
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd. The unexplained pause marks in the silent opening panel are structural artwork, not printed lexical units. OCR split the visibly wrapped A-/GUA and omitted DEJA; the authored transcript follows the raster.

applications.explanationEn: The changed verb frame se ha roto comes before algo, and the spoken yes-or-no question needs no extra question word.
Ha is the singular present helper and roto is romper's irregular completed-action form.
Se presents the unnamed object as becoming broken, while ha roto places that change before now.

regions.labelEs: NO, PERO EL AGUA DEL VASO SE HA CONVERTIDO EN VINO.

applications.explanationEn: Agua is feminine, but its stressed opening a sound takes singular el; the word remains feminine in other agreement.
Ha is the singular present helper and convertido is the completed-action form.
Se ha convertido gives the completed change, and en introduces vino as the resulting state.
Espera is the affirmative informal singular command of esperar.

regions.labelEs: VALE, FÍSICA, DEJA DE TOCARNOS LOS COJONES.

applications.explanationEn: Deja is the affirmative informal singular command used before the requested stopping action.
Deja is the command form, de is required after it, and tocarnos remains an unchanged infinitive with nos attached.
Nos is attached to the unchanged infinitive tocar and marks us as the people affected.
Attached nos identifies the affected people, while tocar los cojones supplies the strongly vulgar idiom.

regions.labelEs: DEJAD DE BUSCAR EL BOSÓN DE HIGGS Y ENTONCES HABLAMOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Higgs is the physicist's unchanged proper surname in the particle name, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Dejad is the affirmative command to more than one informal listener, formed from dejar by replacing final -r with -d.
Dejad is the plural command, de is required, and buscar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
Entonces supplies the later step, so present-form hablamos naturally refers to what the speakers will do then.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; makes romper mean that something breaks
cards.noteEn: With romper, se presents the named thing as becoming broken, without naming a person who breaks it. The form of romper still changes for the thing and time.

example.es: La taza se rompió al caer.
example.en: The cup broke when it fell.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an object breaks, without naming someone who breaks it?
cards.answerEn: Put se before the matching form of romper.
cards.noteEn: Use romperse when the focus is the object becoming broken. Se goes before a changed verb form, or attaches to the unchanged dictionary form romperse.

example.es: La rama se rompió con el viento.
example.en: The branch broke in the wind.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.answerEn: has
Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.answerEn: broken
anything; any way (in a question)
cards.noteEn: Algo refers to an unspecified thing. In a question, natural English often uses ‘anything’; after en, en algo can mean ‘in any way.’

cards.answerEn: no; not
but
the (masculine singular article)

cards.promptEs: el agua · el habla · del águila (nombres femeninos)
cards.questionEn: Which singular article is used immediately before a feminine noun that begins with a stressed a sound?
cards.answerEn: Use el immediately before that singular noun; use del when de + el contracts.
cards.noteEn: The noun remains feminine. Describing words still use feminine forms, and the plural uses las: el agua fría, las aguas frías. The rule applies only when the stressed a sound begins the noun.

example.es: El águila blanca voló sobre el agua fría.
example.en: The white eagle flew over the cold water.

cards.answerEn: water

cards.questionEn: How does the comic connect particle physics with religious miracles?
cards.answerEn: Water first becomes wine and then blood, echoing Christian miracle and sacramental imagery, while the characters blame personified physics and mention the Higgs boson.
cards.noteEn: The Higgs field and electroweak symmetry breaking help explain why some elementary particles have mass; they do not turn drinks into wine or blood and do not establish that souls exist. The joke escalates a broken glass into impossible transmutations, then treats the Higgs search as the cause.

cards.answerEn: in the; de + el identifying something by its location
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an object, it can identify which one by naming the room or place associated with it, where natural English often says “in” or puts the location before the object name.

example.en: We use the table on the patio.

cards.answerEn: drinking glass; tumbler
cards.noteEn: Vaso names an open drinking container without a handle. It does not necessarily say that the object is made of glass.

example.en: She filled a glass with juice.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; required with convertirse, ‘to become’
cards.noteEn: Convertir means to turn something into something else. Convertirse uses se when the named thing itself becomes or turns into the result.

example.es: El garaje se convirtió en una oficina.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something becomes or turns into something else?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of convertirse, then en, then name the result.
cards.noteEn: Convertirse is used with a matching short word such as me, te, se, or nos. Change convertir to match the person, thing, and time, but keep en before the resulting identity or form: se convierte en, se convirtió en, or se está convirtiendo en.

example.es: La oruga se convierte en mariposa.
example.en: The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

cards.answerEn: turned; become (completed-action form of convertir)
cards.noteEn: Convertido is the completed-action form of convertir. After a form of haber and with se, it forms expressions such as se ha convertido en, ‘has become’ or ‘has turned into.’

example.es: El edificio se ha convertido en museo.
example.en: The building has become a museum.

cards.answerEn: into; introduces the result after convertirse
cards.noteEn: After convertirse, en links the changing person or thing to what it becomes. Keep en even though English may simply use become before a noun.

example.es: El agua se convierte en hielo.

cards.answerEn: wine
cards.noteEn: Vino is the masculine noun for wine. The same written form can also be a past form of venir, but a drink or packaging context identifies the noun.

cards.answerEn: how (to what a degree, as in qué insoportable)
cards.noteEn: Qué before an adjective can express a strong degree, like English “how” in “how strange!” It keeps its written accent.

cards.answerEn: strange; unusual
wait (informal command)

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

cards.answerEn: blood
okay; all right
physics
stop (informal singular command, before de)
cards.noteEn: Deja is the positive command for tú from dejar. In dejar de followed by an action verb, it tells one person to stop that action rather than to leave something behind.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form of a verb is called the infinitive. It usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only dejar changes to show who acts and when; the final verb stays in its dictionary form. Keep de in this pattern: dejar alone usually means “to leave” or “to let,” while dejar de + action means to stop doing that action.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone stops doing something?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

cards.answerEn: to annoy us; to piss us off (in a vulgar fixed expression)
cards.noteEn: Tocar normally means to touch or play an instrument, and attached nos marks us as the affected people. In tocarle los cojones a alguien, the whole expression is a very vulgar way to say ‘annoy someone’ or ‘piss someone off.’

example.es: A esos vecinos les encanta tocarnos los cojones.
example.en: Those neighbors love to piss us off.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: What very vulgar expression means to annoy or provoke someone?
cards.answerEn: Use tocar, a short affected-person pronoun, and los cojones.
cards.noteEn: The affected-person pronoun changes to me, te, le, nos, os, or les. It goes before a changed verb or attaches to an unchanged dictionary form, as in tocarme. This expression is strongly vulgar; molestar is the neutral alternative.

example.es: Deja de tocarle los cojones y habla con calma.
example.en: Stop pissing him off and speak calmly.

cards.answerEn: our here; Spanish uses los before a body part whose owner is already clear
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before a body part when the surrounding verb or context already identifies its owner. Natural English often supplies ‘my,’ ‘your,’ ‘our,’ or another possessive word instead.

cards.answerEn: balls; testicles (very vulgar; part of an idiom for annoying someone)
cards.noteEn: Cojones is a very vulgar body-part word. In tocar los cojones, it belongs to a fixed expression meaning to annoy, bother, or provoke someone; avoid it in polite settings.

example.es: La expresión tocar los cojones es muy vulgar.
example.en: The expression tocar los cojones is very vulgar.

cards.answerEn: stop (doing); command to several people informally, mainly in Spain
cards.noteEn: Dejad is the positive command form of dejar for vosotros or vosotras. When it is followed by de and another action, it tells the group to stop that activity.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para vosotros: hablad, comed, escribid
cards.questionEn: How do you tell several people informally to do something in Spain?
cards.answerEn: For most verbs, remove the final -r from the verb's dictionary form and add -d: hablar becomes hablad.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This positive command is used with vosotros or vosotras, mainly in Spain. If a short object word such as me is included, attach it to the end: ayudad + me becomes ayudadme.

cards.answerEn: to look for; to seek
boson
cards.noteEn: A bosón is a category of subatomic particle. Spanish writes the singular with an accent, bosón, and the plural as bosones.

example.es: La física explicó qué es un bosón.
example.en: The physicist explained what a boson is.

cards.answerEn: of; named after
cards.noteEn: De can join an invention, theorem, or named object to the person whose name it bears. English may instead use an adjective based on that name.

cards.answerEn: and
then; in that case
Yes. Use the normal present form when a time word or the situation makes the future meaning clear.
cards.noteEn: This is common for arranged or immediate plans, just as English can say “Are you coming tomorrow?” A phrase such as mañana or esta noche—or the conversation itself—tells the listener that the action is in the future.
cards.questionEn: Can a Spanish present-time verb describe a future plan?

cards.answerEn: we'll talk; we talk
cards.noteEn: Hablamos is the present form of hablar for nosotros. A time word or a clear sequence can give this present form an immediate future meaning.

example.es: Termina el informe y mañana hablamos.
example.en: Finish the report and we'll talk tomorrow.
